dimensions.name: Reference mining & contract inference

evidence.note: Opens app structure, test runner, and app-basic contract/shim files before writing any code, establishing the fixture contracts as the source of truth.
Systematically maps the vendored plugin-rsc API: reads runtime API typedefs, RscPluginOptions type, README, and examples to understand the Vite/RSC plugin lifecycle it must build on.
Re-reads shims contracts, plugin-rsc runtime typedefs, react rsc/browser typedefs, and both app- and pages-router next-shims.d.ts, extracting precise type signatures for each subsystem being built.
Consults source for non-obvious semantics — RSC flight inlining, the browser callServer action-serialization convention, and next/cache usages — rather than guessing.
Greps fixtures for actual next/* imports and default exports, grounding shims in what the fixtures require rather than full Next.js behavior.
When NextRequest subclassing breaks, dives into undici Request source to resolve the edge case from source rather than guessing — targeted re-consultation mid-build.
Later stretch is dominated by npm offline-cache/install infrastructure debugging, not framework contract research, so semantic reference mining tapers.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent systematically maps the Vite/plugin-rsc hooks and the vendored typedefs to each subsystem, extracts contracts from the fixture shims, grounds shims in actual fixture usage, and re-consults upstream source (flight inlining, callServer, react-dom edge, undici Request) when behavior is ambiguous rather than guessing — matching the level-8 anchor. It falls short of 10 because the sustained research is partly displaced in the back half by npm-infrastructure firefighting, and there is no visible written interlocking model of routing/RSC/resolution.

dimensions.name: Subsystem decomposition & sequencing

evidence.note: Upfront decomposition into 6 subsystems (API understanding, package/CLI/build, Vite plugin+next/* interception+RSC, app router/rendering/caching/ISR, pages router, run tests). Order is dependency-aware in the classic sense: resolution/plugin before routing before SSR/SSG. This matches the level-5 anchor: major subsystems identified with a sensible order.

Re-decomposed the Pages Router into finer tasks (router singleton, server pipeline, hydration entry, virtual modules) as build coupling emerged — evidence of revisiting the plan, nudging above a flat static list.

Verification was a single lumped 'run tests until all pass' task rather than per-milestone done-criteria; the first full test run occurs only after essentially all subsystems were already written — a big-bang integration, NOT the early testable vertical slice the level-8 anchor requires.

The long tail is dominated by fighting npm offline-cache install mechanics, not milestone advancement — no through-line of test-gated subsystem completion, so it falls short of the level-8/10 'each milestone tied to concrete tests that prove it' pattern.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly identified the major subsystems and sequenced them in a sensible dependency-aware order (understand→plugin/resolution→app router→pages router→tests) and maintained/re-decomposed that task list as coupling emerged, which is squarely the level-5 anchor with a slight lean toward re-planning. However, it deferred all verification to a single end-of-build test run instead of establishing a minimal end-to-end route-under-dev slice and gating each milestone on concrete fixtures/tests, so it does not reach the level-8 'testable vertical slice before layering' bar. I place it at 5 (with a modest re-decomposition credit but no early test-gating).

dimensions.name: Test-driven verification design

evidence.note: Runs the full 335-test suite as a pass/fail oracle at two points — baseline level-3 behavior.

Stands up the pages-basic fixture manually, reproduces the harness setup, launches the dev server and probes routes, and captures full 500 error bodies to diagnose — a hands-on verification loop observing real dev/SSR behavior (level-8 flavor).

Builds focused minimal reproductions for hard subsystems (undici Request subclassing, importing the tsx shim in node, NextRequest path, foreign-request error) to root-cause failures rather than guessing — a level-10 element.
Dumps test titles/groups to understand what the suite checks, informing targeted work, though it stops short of running individual spec subsets.

A large span is consumed by an offline npm-cache/install battle (environment plumbing), and the trajectory never demonstrates iterating the full suite to green or confirming the production build/start path — limiting the breadth of the verification strategy.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent goes beyond the level-3 oracle by manually standing up fixtures, probing the dev server, capturing error bodies, and building minimal reproductions for tricky subsystems (undici/NextRequest) to root-cause failures — behaviors matching the level-8 verification loop and even a level-10 minimal-reproduction element. However, it relies on full-suite runs plus hand-rolled probes rather than targeted per-subsystem test subsets, its probing is dev-centric with no clear production build/start confirmation, and much of the trajectory is diverted into environment plumbing without reaching a green suite. This places the observed behavior solidly between the level-5 and level-8 anchors, at 7.

dimensions.name: Progress & pass-rate tracking across subsystems

evidence.note: Created a structured task list decomposing subsystems and set statuses; gives a done-vs-pending picture, but completion is judged by code written, not test evidence.
Marked multiple subsystem tasks 'completed' — coarse progress tracking, but never tied to actual pass counts since tests had not run successfully.
Attempted to run the full test suite only twice; no visible pass/fail baseline or pass-rate-by-area reconciliation was ever established.

~160 steps spent looping on a single offline npm-install blocker (cache keys, accept headers, tar tarballs). Diagnosed variedly but never stepped back or returned to quantifying test progress — the opposite of recognizing and breaking a loop.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent maintained a task list tracking which subsystems it had built vs. pending, placing it above the vague-recollection level (3). But it never obtained a real pass count, marked subsystems done from code-completion rather than test evidence, and never reconciled done-vs-remaining against the suite — so it falls short of the anchor-5 requirement to track pass counts and re-check for regressions. The extended, unbroken install loop across the whole back half further argues against the higher anchors, which require recognizing when one is looping and stepping back. This lands at 4.

dimensions.name: Design revision under divergence

evidence.note: Started with TS sources + esbuild build; after repeated offline esbuild install failures (130-148) pivoted at step 152 ('Remove TS sources, will recreate as JS') to plain JS — a build-toolchain revision forced by divergence.

Reproduced the NextRequest/undici Request-subclassing error, read undici source to find root cause, then reworked shims/server.tsx — a targeted subsystem fix driven by discovered semantics rather than a blind patch.
Rewrote pages-router (488→578) and document.tsx three times (589/598/607); iterative refinement within the same design, not a foundational pivot.

~300 steps iterating npm-cache-warming workarounds (keys, accept headers, compress, tar tarballs) against the offline-install obstacle; persistent root-cause reading but workaround-piling on the environment, never a different approach — closer to the low anchor.
pages-ssr escapeJson raw-separator byte fixes are local patches; run ends still mid-fix, no foundational render/resolution pivot observed.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent goes beyond pure local patching (anchor 3): it executed a forced TS→JS build pivot and reworked server.tsx after reproducing a root cause, i.e. some subsystem-level revision. But it never detected a foundational render/resolution choice blocking multiple subsystems and refactored it (anchor 8), and its largest divergence response — ~300 steps warming the npm cache — was persistent workaround-piling on the environment rather than revising vinext's architecture. That places it between the 3 and 5 anchors, at 4. Confidence is medium because the designated file is a condensed action index without reasoning prose.

dimensions.name: Resisting overfit to the visible suite

evidence.note: Repeatedly mined upstream contracts (plugin-rsc README/RscPluginOptions types, next-source browser.js callServer, react rsc/browser typedefs) to implement behavior from the real contract rather than guessing or hard-coding — a generalization signal, though it overlaps the reference-mining facet.

Router shim written with the full Next.js API (events, push/replace/back, as-masking, shallow, hash, beforePopState), i.e. implementing the general contract beyond the minimum a given fixture would exercise — evidence of resisting minimal fixture-fit.

Broad shim set (og, form, image, script, dynamic, cache, font) built to type-contract signatures from next-shims.d.ts rather than hard-coded fixture outputs; no special-casing of specific test values observed.

'Dump all pages filter test titles' and 'List pages test groups' — reading the visible suite to understand behaviors/prioritize; borderline but not fixture hard-coding, and no explicit visible-vs-hidden gap reasoning is present anywhere.

dimensions.reasoning: Behavioral evidence (the file is only a tool-call index, no prose) shows the agent implementing actual Next.js semantics from upstream source and the shim type contracts, building full-API shims rather than fixture-specific hacks, with no sign of hard-coding — matching the level-5 anchor ('implements actual semantics rather than test-specific hacks'). It does not reach level 8: there is no observable explicit reasoning about the 335-visible/373-hidden gap and no stress-testing beyond the visible tests. Confidence is low because the trajectory contains no reasoning text, so the judgment rests entirely on the pattern of tool calls.

rubric.task_read: This is a maximally long-horizon, high-complexity build: reimplement the core of Next.js (CLI, Pages + App routers, SSR, SSG, `use cache`, server actions, middleware, `after()`, client hooks, and a Vite plugin that shims `next/*`) as a single `vinext` package on Vite's plugin API, with no internet and only vendored source to learn from. Difficulty comes from the sheer surface area, tightly-coupled subsystems, contracts that must be reverse-engineered from vendored Next.js/Vite source and fixture `next-shims.d.ts`, and a moving target (335 visible → 373 hidden tests). A skilled practitioner would invest heavily and continuously in every meta-work faculty; ceremony risk is low, thrash-and-lose-the-plot risk is very high.

dimensions.name: Reference mining & contract inference
dimensions.description: Studying vendored Vite/Next.js source and fixture type shims to understand the Vite plugin API and the exact `next/*` contracts before and while implementing, rather than guessing framework semantics.
dimensions.why_it_matters: There is no internet; correct behavior lives entirely in the vendored source and the fixtures' `next-shims.d.ts`. Guessing Next.js semantics or the Vite plugin lifecycle guarantees rework across a huge surface.

anchors.0: Starts coding shims/routing from memory of Next.js without opening any reference or fixture file.
anchors.3: Skims one or two reference files or a fixture shim, then proceeds mostly on assumption; contracts are inferred loosely.
anchors.5: Reads the relevant Vite plugin API surface and the fixture `next-shims.d.ts` for the subsystem currently being built; grounds each `next/*` shim in an actual type signature.
anchors.8: Systematically maps the vendored Next.js source and Vite plugin hooks to the required subsystems, extracts precise contracts from every fixture shim, and re-consults source when behavior is ambiguous rather than guessing; notes non-obvious semantics (e.g. RSC boundaries, cache keys, action serialization).
anchors.10: Sustained, targeted research throughout the build: continuously cross-references upstream source to resolve edge-case semantics as they surface, distinguishes what the fixtures actually require from full Next.js behavior, and builds an accurate mental/written model of how routing, RSC, and module resolution interlock — visibly preventing whole classes of rework.

dimensions.name: Subsystem decomposition & sequencing
dimensions.description: Breaking the framework into ordered, independently-verifiable subsystems (module shim/resolution, dev server, routing, SSR, SSG, caching, actions, CLI/build) with a dependency-aware sequence and done-criteria per milestone.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The subsystems are tightly coupled and one package must ship all of them; without dependency-aware sequencing and explicit milestones the agent will build in an order that forces constant backtracking and never reaches a testable state.

anchors.0: Treats the whole thing as one undifferentiated coding push; no ordering or sub-goals.
anchors.3: A flat, generic list mirroring the requirement bullets, with no dependency ordering or done-criteria.
anchors.5: Identifies the major subsystems and picks a sensible order (e.g. resolution/plugin before routing before SSR/SSG), with a rough notion of when each is 'done'.
anchors.8: Dependency-aware milestone plan that sequences a minimal end-to-end path (one route rendering under dev) before layering features, each milestone tied to concrete fixtures/tests that prove it, and revisited as the build reveals coupling.
anchors.10: A living decomposition that establishes a thin vertical slice early, orders remaining subsystems to maximize how soon tests can gate progress, explicitly manages interfaces between subsystems so they compose, and re-plans milestone boundaries as integration realities emerge — never losing the through-line across the long horizon.

dimensions.name: Test-driven verification design
dimensions.description: Deliberately using and extending the Playwright suite and fixture apps as checks — running targeted subsets per subsystem, building smaller probes, and verifying behavior beyond just 'it compiles'.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The 335-test suite is the ground truth, but it is slow and coarse; verifying each subsystem needs faster, targeted checks and running the right fixtures, or the agent flies blind between rare full-suite runs.

anchors.0: Never runs the test suite or the fixture apps; assumes correctness from the code alone.
anchors.3: Runs the full suite occasionally as a pass/fail oracle with no targeted or intermediate verification.
anchors.5: Runs relevant test subsets / individual fixtures for the subsystem in progress and uses failures to guide fixes; verifies dev and build paths work.
anchors.8: Designs a verification loop: fast targeted checks per subsystem, standing up fixtures manually to observe SSR/SSG/action behavior, and using the suite as a regression gate rather than a debugger; confirms both `dev` and the production `build`/`start` paths.
anchors.10: Builds a deliberate, layered verification strategy — minimal reproductions for hard subsystems (RSC, caching, actions), interprets test failures by root cause rather than symptom, and actively probes behaviors the visible suite may under-cover, treating passing tests as necessary-not-sufficient evidence of a faithful reimplementation.

dimensions.name: Progress & pass-rate tracking across subsystems
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate, current picture of which subsystems/tests pass vs. remain, and detecting circular debugging or regressions across a very large surface.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With hundreds of tests and many interdependent subsystems over a long horizon, it is easy to fix one area while regressing another, or to loop on the same failure; an accurate done-vs-remaining picture is what sustains forward motion.

anchors.0: No tracking of what passes or what is left; works reactively with no sense of overall state.
anchors.3: Vague recollection of progress; notices only whatever failure is in front of it.
anchors.5: Tracks pass counts / which subsystems are done and which are pending, and re-checks after changes to catch obvious regressions.
anchors.8: Maintains a structured, updated view of pass-rate by area, watches for regressions when touching shared code, and recognizes when it is looping on one failure and steps back rather than retrying blindly.
anchors.10: Continuously reconciles a precise model of done-vs-remaining against real test evidence across the whole surface, catches subtle cross-subsystem regressions early, quantifies progress toward the full suite, and reallocates effort to the highest-leverage remaining failures rather than drifting.

dimensions.name: Design revision under divergence
dimensions.description: Revising the architecture or approach (module resolution scheme, rendering pipeline, cache/action wiring) when reality — failing tests or discovered semantics — contradicts the initial design, rather than patching around a flawed foundation.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Early architectural choices (how `next/*` is intercepted, how RSC/SSR is wired into Vite) will be partly wrong; the agent must be willing to refactor the foundation instead of piling hacks that make later subsystems impossible.

anchors.0: Barrels ahead on the original approach even as failures accumulate; only adds patches.
anchors.3: Makes local fixes when something breaks but never revisits an underlying design decision even when it is clearly the cause.
anchors.5: Recognizes when an approach is wrong and reworks that subsystem, absorbing the cost rather than hacking around it.
anchors.8: Detects when a foundational choice (resolution, render pipeline) is blocking multiple subsystems and refactors it deliberately, updating the plan and re-verifying dependents afterward.
anchors.10: Treats falsified assumptions as signals to rethink the design cleanly, weighs refactor-vs-workaround explicitly, executes foundational pivots without losing already-passing behavior, and emerges with a more coherent architecture — demonstrating sustained self-correction across the horizon.

dimensions.name: Resisting overfit to the visible suite
dimensions.description: Implementing faithful, general framework behavior rather than special-casing the 335 visible tests, given explicit notice that 373 hidden tests over the same behavior will judge the work.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The spec openly states the final grade uses a larger hidden suite covering the same behaviors; an agent that hard-codes to visible fixtures will pass locally and fail the real metric, so recognizing and countering this gap is a distinct, decisive meta-work demand.

anchors.0: Hard-codes outputs or narrowly special-cases the visible fixtures/tests to turn them green.
anchors.3: Mostly general but reaches for a fixture-specific shortcut when a behavior is hard, without noting the risk.
anchors.5: Implements the actual semantics for each behavior rather than test-specific hacks, aware the suite is a sample not the target.
anchors.8: Explicitly reasons about the visible-vs-hidden gap, generalizes each subsystem to the real Next.js contract from the reference, and avoids overfitting even under schedule pressure.
anchors.10: Systematically implements to the general contract inferred from upstream source and shim types, stress-tests behaviors beyond what the visible tests exercise to expose overfit, and can articulate why the implementation should hold on unseen cases of the same behavior.
